[about 50 seconds] Before I show you the new equipment, a minute on why it is here. This is joint work between the School of Psychology and Computing and Informatics, across three projects. MosAIcSOC, which I coordinate and lead as PI, is a 5.9 million euro EU project building an AI-enabled framework for Security Operations Centres: a shared data model, a secure app store, digital twins to rehearse incident response, and federated learning so organisations can collaborate without sharing raw data. SCIFER, where I am co-investigator, is another 5.9 million euro EU project on smarter cybersecurity for critical infrastructure: detect risks earlier, respond smarter. And here at BU, the SOC of the Future, funded with nearly 2.3 million pounds from the Office for Students, where John McAlaney from our department is Co-Investigator. Different funders, different consortia, but they all circle the same thing: an AI-powered security operations centre.

What the projects share

Three essential components

Psychology and cyberpsychology sit here

Every overlap with the gold circle is a human question

[about 40 seconds] Every one of these projects is built from the same three components, in line with the EU Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI. The Security Operations Centre itself: people, process and telemetry. Agentic AI: the agents and tools doing more and more of the detection and remediation. And the human in the loop: judgement and accountability. That gold circle is us. It is where psychology and cyberpsychology sit. And notice that it is not a separate box at the side. It overlaps the other two: the skills analysts need to work with AI, and the question of how much access and trust the AI should be given.

The common denominator

Every one of these SOCs
is AI-powered

So the interaction between the human and the AI becomes the critical part, and it is still largely unknown.

[about 35 seconds] Here is the point I want you to take away. All three projects are AI-powered. Once that is true, the weakest and least understood link is no longer the technology and no longer the analyst alone. It is what happens between them. When does an analyst trust the agent too much? When do they stop checking? When do they start treating it as a colleague rather than a tool? Engineers cannot answer those questions. We can. But only if we can measure that interaction, and until recently we had very little to measure it with.

[about 50 seconds] So we started building the measurement tools ourselves, and there is now a battery. The first is LLM-D12. We were the first research team to develop a behavioural assessment of LLM dependency based on two types. Instrumental dependency is leaning on the model for decisions and cognitive work. Relationship dependency is treating it as a social, companion-like entity. It is published in ACM Transactions on the Web. The second is PT-LLM-8, perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, covering eight dimensions: truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, transparency, accountability and compliance with laws. The third is a set of four AI apprehension scales, which separate apprehension towards personal AI, general AI, institutional AI and large language models. And this is the point: these are not niche tools. Our measure is included in the world’s largest survey on digital wellbeing, the Ithra Sync survey supported by Aramco, running in 50 countries with more than 50,000 respondents, and with teams internationally it is being translated and applied to very diverse populations. Dependency, trust and apprehension: together they tell us how a person relates to AI.

Why the new equipment matters

Linking the battery to psychophysiology

What people report

Battery

What the body does

Heart · Skin · Breath · Face

Responses moment by moment

Do people high in dependency or trust respond differently, in body and face, when the AI gets it wrong?

[about 40 seconds] But a questionnaire, however well validated, tells us what people report about themselves. It captures stable differences between people: this analyst is more dependent, that one trusts the system less. It does not tell us what happens in the moment, when an AI agent makes a recommendation and the person has two seconds to accept it or challenge it. That is the link we can now make. On one side, the battery. On the other, psychophysiology: heart, skin, breathing and the face, recorded moment by moment. Put them together, in the same person and the same session, and we can ask questions nobody has been able to ask. For example: do people who score high on dependency or trust respond differently when the AI gets it wrong? Do they even notice? That is what the new equipment is for.

[about 40 seconds] So, the equipment. We now have iMotions licences for three years, and with them three sets of wearable sensors. A heart rate monitor, which gives us heart rate and heart rate variability. A skin conductance sensor, which picks up arousal moment by moment. And a breathing band, for respiration rate and depth. Three of each, so we can record three people at once: for example a small SOC team working an incident together with an AI agent. iMotions records all three streams on one timeline, synchronised with whatever is on the screen.

What we can measure

From sensor to psychological construct

SensorSignalMeasures derivedWhat it indexes
Heart rate monitorCardiacHeart rate, inter-beat interval, HRVAutonomic regulation, effort, stress
Skin conductanceElectrodermalTonic level, phasic response peaksSympathetic arousal, event by event
Breathing bandRespiratoryBreathing rate and depthLoad and regulation; context for HRV
OCOsense glassesFacial skin movementExpression intensity, valence, engagementPositive or negative response
Psychometric batterySelf-reportDependency, trust, apprehension scoresHow a person relates to AI
[about 40 seconds] For those who want the technical picture, this is the chain from sensor to construct. The heart rate monitor gives us the cardiac signal, and from that heart rate, the inter-beat interval and heart rate variability, which index autonomic regulation, effort and stress. Skin conductance separates a slow tonic level from fast phasic peaks, so we get sympathetic arousal locked to individual events: an alert appearing, an AI recommendation arriving. The breathing band gives rate and depth, which is informative in itself and also needed to interpret heart rate variability properly. Arousal alone does not tell us whether a reaction is good or bad, and that is what the glasses add: expression intensity and valence. And the battery gives us the person's own account. No single channel is enough; the value is in having them together.

Why this kit

Five practical advantages

Accurate

Research-grade signal quality

[about 35 seconds] Why this kit rather than a traditional psychophysiology lab? Five reasons. There are no wires, so people can move, type and work normally. The analysis is instantaneous: signals are synchronised and processed as they come in, so you can see what is happening during the session, not weeks later. It records continuously for up to five hours, which is long enough for a realistic working session rather than a ten-minute lab task. It is non-intrusive: once it is on, participants largely forget about it. And the accuracy is research grade. Together that means we can take measurement out of the cubicle and into something that looks like real work.

[about 40 seconds] The second piece of equipment is three pairs of Emteq OCOsense glasses. They look and wear like ordinary glasses, 83 grams, but the frame carries six optical sensors that track the movement of the skin over key facial muscles, at a resolution below five micrometres, fifty times a second. From that the system gives us expression intensity, valence, so positive versus negative response, and engagement. There is also a motion sensor, so we know whether the person is sitting, walking or turning their head. They are completely untethered, streaming over Bluetooth, with up to four hours of battery. So where the iMotions sensors tell us how activated someone is, the glasses tell us whether that activation is positive or negative, without pointing a camera at them.

[about 40 seconds] So, to bring it together. We now have three kinds of measure for the same person in the same session. What people say, with the psychometric battery. What the body does: heart, skin and breathing. And what the face shows, with the glasses. Together they let us study how people actually react, how they make decisions, how they interact with a large language model and how far they rely on it. That is true for LLM use in general: everyday work, study and decision making. And it is true in particular for the situation our projects care about most, a cyberattack, where an analyst is working with an AI agent under time pressure and the cost of misplaced trust is very high. We have three sets of everything, so three people can be recorded at once, and the iMotions licences run for three years. If you have a study or a student project in mind, come and talk to me. Thank you.
